And literal colonization. Not a dozen or so scientists digging through the dirt but a self sufficient civilization of hundreds of thousands developing in parallel to Earth.

So facts and information. The 27th of this month is a huge date and one that many have been anticipating for years. There is a major intentional aerospace conference going on - The International Astronautical Congress. Elon Musk will be giving a talk there on colonizing Mars where the architecture for getting us there is expected to be revealed. In particular they are working towards the development of the MCT or Mars Colonial Transporter. These are going to be massive ships, vastly massive than anything we've ever put into space, that will carry up to 100 astronaut settlers at a time. It's going to sound insane, kind of like putting poles carrying thousands of volts up everywhere in a country that pans hundreds of milliones of acres so everybody can have electricity, would have sounded insane.

2018 is another big date. 2018 marks the day that SpaceX will be sending the first privately launched rocket to Mars. There should be some interesting payloads on there because of the next big date. 2024 is the target date for SpaceX to send the first humans to a different planet. This first group will obviously not be mainstream settlers, but highly specialized and trained astronauts expanding and developing the infrastructure that will have already been laid down by other flights. Between 2018 and 2024 there are only 3 flights available as Mars and Earth's orbits only align during a period that occurs once about every 2 years. So there should be some extremely interesting experiments being rolled out extremely rapidly. For instance I would not be surprised to see food experiments to be included on their 2018 launch. Imagine seeing the first food, the first Earthen life, grow on Mars. The symbolism alone is incredible.

Back on the 2 year alignment issues - there's no such thing as a quick hop and back home on Mars. By the time you get there the fastest you will be able to get back is after you spend the better part of a year on the planet and the orbits realign. The closest Mars get and the furthest it gets differ by a factor of about 8x meaning once you're there - you're there. So visiting Mars at all entails setting up long-term settlements. NASA is an interesting factor here. On paper they're stated date for humans to Mars is the mid 2030s. However, if you follow their actions they are extremely rapidly revving up and doing research that doesn't exactly make sense for that date. For instance as early as 2010 they commissioned an MIT study on the most efficient means of energy of production specifically for a Martian colony. Given the rapid evolutions energy production is making, that's not generally something you'd be studying if you were planning on going the better part of 3 decades later.

Finally there is also international competition coming into play here that should help ensure we remain focused even outside of SpaceX. China, Europe (the European Space Agency), Russia, and other countries have all stated intentions to put men on the moon and continue expanding their programs to begin experimenting with Mars as well. We're far ahead of the world for now in things like this, but unless we continue pushing it - it's going to become yet another thing that we were far ahead of the world in. But this one is rather more visible and would have potential implications in national security and propaganda. In other words, I think we're going to stay focused.

This all is just scratching the surface of what's going on - but yeah there are some incredibly exciting things happening and this is likely to only accelerate during our lifetimes. Unless you pull a Ritchie Valens on us, you're going to see humans living on different planets.
